frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d8: Prime Minister Winston Churchill wrote to President Roosevelt on June 13, 1943, in a message preserved as Document 8 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Churchill and Roosevelt wrote to each other constantly through the war, often daily. The catalog record for this item gives the date and the two men only. Its place in the volume, among papers leading to Cairo and Tehran, is the surest guide to the world it came from.
frus-1944-quebec-d8:
President Roosevelt wrote to Prime Minister Churchill on May 31, 1944, closing the month's exchange six days before D-Day. The message appears in the State Department's Quebec 1944 volume.

By May 31 the invasion was set in motion and could not be recalled. The leaders' correspondence in those days mixed last military questions with the politics that would follow liberation. Roosevelt's end-of-May message belongs to that threshold. For readers, it marks the point where the planning written across the Cairo, Tehran, and Quebec volumes began to turn into action on the beaches of Normandy.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d8: Roosevelt turned to Churchill on 4 October 1944, writing to the British prime minister the same day he instructed Harriman. The letter is document 8 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on Malta and Yalta. Anglo-American messages like this one coordinated the two Western allies before either of them sat down with Stalin at the next summit conference.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d8:
Grew's memorandum of May 14, 1945, records a White House conference with Eden and Attlee present. At the President's wish, the Acting Secretary attended the meeting between Truman, Eden, Attlee, John Balfour, and Admiral Leahy. Two subjects surface in the extracts: the Polish problem, and a meeting of the Big Three.

On Poland, Eden felt no solution could be expected until the President, the Prime Minister, and Stalin could meet. The Prime Minister hoped such a meeting could take place as early as possible. Truman answered that, having been brought unexpectedly into the job, he had many difficulties to contend with. The memorandum shows the new President being briefed by both British parties at once.
tob-0039-d8:
The ninth microfilm roll of the Doctors' Trial transcript preserves more of the Nuremberg case heard in 1946 and 1947. American judges tried doctors and officials accused of murderous experiments on camp inmates. The transcript was kept verbatim, then filmed for permanent record.

This roll carries the proceedings forward through further evidence and argument on the medical crimes charged. Survivors' accounts and captured documents sit side by side in the record. The trial's judgment helped produce the Nuremberg Code, the ten points that still govern research on human subjects. For readers who want the case unfiltered, the rolls give the testimony as the court received it.
podcast-joerogan-Eq4y2vh8TD8: Sarko Gergerian joins Joe Rogan for episode 2357 of the Joe Rogan Experience, the long-form talk show Rogan hosts from his studio. The record kept with the file gives the guest name and the episode number but no topic line, no guest background, and no summary of the talk. The file holds the full transcript of that sitting in the show's free, wide-ranging form. Listeners will learn the ground covered only from the talk itself, since the record states nothing more.
podcast-joerogan-A9zS94x2nd8:
Wim Hof, the Dutch athlete called the Iceman, leads Rogan through his breathing method in an excerpt from episode 712 of the Joe Rogan Experience. Hof built fame on enduring extreme cold and teaching others his breath work. Here the lesson happens on the show itself.

Rogan breathes along as Hof counts the rounds and explains what the practice does to blood, nerves, and mood. The excerpt mixes instruction with Hof's life story of loss and discipline. Listeners can follow the method in real time, which makes this entry part interview and part guided session, a rare how-to moment for the show.
frus-1945-50-intel-d8:
Hoover wrote to Attorney General Clark again on 6 September 1945, the second Hoover letter in the volume within eight days. The pace marks the FBI's close watch on the intelligence plans then moving in Washington. The text comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States volume that looks back at American intelligence work from 1945 to 1950.

Hoover believed foreign intelligence in the Americas belonged to his bureau, and he said so up his chain of command whenever plans stirred. Writing to the attorney general put his case before the one cabinet officer who could carry it to the president. Readers following the FBI thread will find Hoover consistent from first to last. The bureau's wartime gains were not to be given up without a fight. This letter is part of that fight's opening.
frus-1861-d8:
Joseph Wright reported to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 26 May 1861. The dispatch is document 8 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Late May brought word that Britain would treat the Confederacy as a belligerent, though not as a nation. Every American post in Europe had to answer that step in its own court. Wright's letter is one voice in that wide response, filed from his post and kept in the official record. Posts like his had to answer at once, in talks with local ministers who pressed for the Union's view.
frus-1862-d8:
17 January 1862 is stamped on a letter Seward got from Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. The printed record keeps it as Document 8 in the 1862 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs volume. The date falls in the winter of the war's second year, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

The text is the view from the post abroad: local mood, official talk, and the envoy's own judgment. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1863p1-d8:
Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Charles Francis Adams on 30 November 1862, the same day as his other letter in this part of the volume. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 8 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

Two letters in one day let Seward split the London brief: one for the broad line, one for the point at hand. His mail to Adams had to guide a man who dealt daily with Lord Russell and the British cabinet. This letter is one of those paired sheets, a small part of the closest-run exchange in the whole wartime file.
